Special Cases and Simulation Verification

Source: vignettes/special-cases-and-simulation.Rmd
special-cases-and-simulation.Rmd

This vignette places the procedures of the package beside one another: the one stopping rule behind the accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) family, the fixed sample size planners in DMAR that answer the same question when a population value can be supposed, two simulations that show where the asymptotic guarantee holds and where it does not, the classical procedures with what each one guarantees, and the budget constrained procedure.

One Stopping Rule, Many Effect Sizes

Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018) define a general family of effect sizes, the ratio of two parameters that are each a function of one or more other parameters (their Equation 1), estimated by the same ratio with U-statistics in place of the parameters (their Equation 4), and they give one sequential procedure for the whole family. Write ω for the target full width of the confidence interval, z for the standard normal quantile of the confidence level (1.96 at 0.95), and Vn2 for the estimate, computed from the first n observations, of the asymptotic variance ξ2 of √n times the estimator. Sampling begins with a pilot sample of the larger of m0 and 2z/ω (rounded up) observations (their Equation 21; m0 is 4 by default in the package) and stops at the first n with

n ≥ (2z / ω)2 (Vn2 + 1 / n)

(their Equation 22). The interval reported there is the estimate plus and minus z Vn / √n (their Equation 23). The term 1 / n keeps the rule from being met too early on a variance estimate that happens to be small. What changes from one effect size to the next is the estimator and its variance estimate; the pilot rule, the stopping rule, and the form of the interval do not. Neither does the guarantee: the interval at the stopping point is never wider than ω, and its coverage approaches the confidence level as ω shrinks (their Theorem 2). At a wide target the coverage can fall well short, as a later section shows.

Effect size Function Sequential procedure Fixed sample size planner in DMAR
Standardized mean difference seq_aipe_smd() Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2018, Example 1) ss_aipe_smd()
Coefficient of variation seq_aipe_cv() 2018, Example 2 ss_aipe_cv()
Standardized mean seq_aipe_sm() 2018, Example 3 ss_aipe_sm()
Slope of a simple linear regression seq_aipe_reg_coef() 2018, Example 4 ss_aipe_reg_coef()
Contrast of group means seq_aipe_c() 2018, Example 6 ss_aipe_c()
Pearson correlation seq_aipe_r(method = "pearson") Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2019) ss_aipe_r()
Kendall’s τ and Spearman’s ρ seq_aipe_r(method = "kendall"), seq_aipe_r(method = "spearman") 2019 None
Gini index seq_aipe_gini() Chattopadhyay & De (2016) None
Squared multiple correlation seq_aipe_R2() 2019 ss_aipe_R2()

The first five rows are among the 2018 article’s examples of members of the family; it works three of them through in detail (the standardized mean difference, the coefficient of variation, and the regression slope). The correlation coefficients are treated in the 2019 article with a rule of the same form. The Gini index procedure is that of Chattopadhyay and De (2016), whose rule also has this form once their half width is written as ω / 2; the 2018 article cites it and contains no Gini index procedure of its own. The squared multiple correlation is the exception in the table. Its interval rests on the normal theory variance of the sample squared multiple correlation, so it assumes multivariate normal data, and it has a stopping rule of its own (see ?seq_aipe_R2).

The family of the 2018 article is wider than the table. Cliff’s delta for ordinal data (their Example 5) and single parameters such as a mean, a variance, or Gini’s mean difference (their Example 7) belong to it and have no seq_aipe_*() function here (DMAR plans a fixed sample size for Cliff’s delta with ss_aipe_cliff_delta()). A mean is covered by one of the classical functions described below: seq_fwd_dfr_mean() applies the rule above with the sample variance as Vn2 and ω equal to twice its half width d.

set.seed(113)
scores <- rnorm(150, mean = 70, sd = 8)  # simulated scores, used again below
d <- 2                                   # half width, so the full width is 4
check <- seq_fwd_dfr_mean(scores[1:40], d = d)
z <- qnorm(0.975)
c(package = attr(check, "criterion_n"),
  equation_22 = ceiling((2 * z / (2 * d))^2 * (var(scores[1:40]) + 1 / 40)))
#>     package equation_22 
#>          66          66

seq_budget() (Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal, 2025) is a companion to this family and not a member of it: it ends when a fixed budget has been spent as well as the data allow, not when an interval reaches a target width. The last section returns to it.

Fixed Sample Size Counterparts in DMAR

When a value of the population effect size can be supposed in advance, the sample size can be fixed in advance, and that is what the ss_aipe_*() functions of DMAR do. The table above names the counterpart of each sequential function; the rank correlations and the Gini index have none. The two kinds of function take different inputs.

  • DMAR::ss_aipe_smd(delta, conf_level = 0.95, width, assurance = NULL) takes a supposed population value delta and returns the sample size per group at which the expected width of the confidence interval is no more than width (with assurance, the size at which the realized width is no more than width with that probability). It needs no data.
  • seq_aipe_smd(group_1, group_2, width, conf_level = 0.95) takes the data collected so far and reports whether the stopping rule is met. It needs no supposed value, and the final sample size is not known until sampling ends.

The DMAR planners rest on normal theory intervals (for the correlation, the Fisher z interval), while the sequential procedures, the squared multiple correlation aside, estimate the variance without assuming a distribution, so the two do not plan for the identical interval. They answer the same design question under different assumptions.

How much the supposed value matters depends on the effect size.

plan_smd <- function(delta) {
  plan <- DMAR::ss_aipe_smd(delta = delta, width = 0.4)
  plan$value[plan$term == "necessary_n_per_group"]
}
plan_r <- function(rho) {
  plan <- DMAR::ss_aipe_r(rho = rho, width = 0.2)
  plan$value[plan$term == "necessary_N"]
}
supposed <- c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8)
plans <- data.frame(supposed_value = supposed,
                    smd_n_per_group = sapply(supposed, plan_smd),
                    correlation_n_pairs = sapply(supposed, plan_r))
plans
#>   supposed_value smd_n_per_group correlation_n_pairs
#> 1            0.2             194                 355
#> 2            0.5             199                 219
#> 3            0.8             208                  56

For a standardized mean difference and a width of 0.4, the plan moves from 194 to 208 per group as the supposed value goes from 0.2 to 0.8. For a correlation and a width of 0.2, it moves from 355 pairs to 56: a researcher who supposes 0.5 when the population value is 0.2 plans 219 pairs where 355 are needed, and the interval comes out wider than planned. A sequential procedure removes the supposed value. The price is a sample size that is not known in advance and, as the simulations below show, a confidence level that can be trusted only when the target is narrow enough for the true value.

The case for planning a sample size for a narrow confidence interval, and not for statistical power alone, is made in Kelley and Maxwell (2003), Kelley and Rausch (2006), and Maxwell, Kelley, and Rausch (2008). The sequential procedures of this package are developed in Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, 2017), Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, 2019), and Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025).

A Simulation Check: The Standardized Mean Difference

Each seq_aipe_*() check function has a _sensitivity companion that runs the whole procedure many times against a population whose effect size is known (for the correlation, the companion studies the Pearson coefficient). For a true standardized mean difference of 0.5 and a target width of 0.4, in a study that can check the rule only after every 10 participants per group:

smd_sim <- seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, width = 0.4,
                                    G = 200, seed = 113, batch = 10)
smd_sim
#> term                   value
#> true_value             0.5
#> target_width           0.4
#> conf_level             0.95
#> replications           200
#> mean_n                 203.6
#> median_n               200
#> sd_n                   6.652917
#> mean_width             0.3946013
#> median_width           0.3945118
#> pct_width_within       100
#> coverage               0.935
#> pct_hit_max_n          0
#> pct_variance_unusable  0

The width guarantee holds by construction: pct_width_within is 100, so no final interval was wider than the target. The mean final sample size was 203.6 per group. If the population value were known to be 0.5, DMAR::ss_aipe_smd(delta = 0.5, width = 0.4) would plan 199 per group. The sequential procedure, which is told nothing about the population value, ended 4.6 per group above that on average. That is what checking only after every 10 costs, about half a batch: checked after every observation (batch = 1, the default), the same design ended at a mean of 199.1 per group in the replications reported in the Details of ?seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity.

The final interval contained the true value in 93.5 percent of the 200 replications. The Monte Carlo standard error of that proportion is 1.7 percentage points, so a simulation of this size detects a gross failure and nothing finer: it cannot tell a coverage of 0.95 from one of 0.93. A planning result that will be reported deserves many more replications. In 4,700 to 6,000 replications of this design at each of four batch sizes, coverage was between 0.949 and 0.952 (the same Details, ?seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity).

A Cautionary Simulation: The Pearson Correlation at a Wide Target

The same check for the Pearson correlation, at a width chosen to be wide for the true value, shows what the asymptotic guarantee does not promise.

r_sim <- seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, width = 0.5,
                                G = 200, seed = 113)
r_sim
#> term                   value
#> true_value             0.5
#> target_width           0.5
#> conf_level             0.95
#> replications           200
#> mean_n                 26.42
#> median_n               21
#> sd_n                   15.13336
#> mean_width             0.377283
#> median_width           0.4418572
#> pct_width_within       100
#> coverage               0.67
#> pct_hit_max_n          0
#> pct_variance_unusable  38

The pilot sample is 8 pairs. For bivariate normal data ξ2 is (1 − ρ2)2, so the sample size the rule aims at, (2z / ω)2 ξ2, is 34.6 pairs. The procedure stopped at a mean of 26.4. Every final interval was within the target width, and only 67 percent of them contained the true correlation (Monte Carlo standard error 3 percentage points), where 95 percent was asked for.

Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019) report this behavior and trace it in their Appendix D: the variance estimate is built from ratios of unbiased moment estimates, a ratio of unbiased estimates is not itself unbiased, and in small samples the variance tends to be underestimated. The rule is then met too early, and the interval keeps its width without keeping its coverage.

The row pct_variance_unusable shows a second symptom. In 38 percent of the replications the variance estimate was zero or negative at one or more checks. A check of that kind has estimated no variance, and the package reports its stopping rule as not met, with the attribute variance_unusable set to TRUE and a printed note (see “An Unusable Variance Estimate” in help("SMSD-package")). That is a deliberate departure from the stopping rule as printed, which would stop at once with an interval far narrower than the data support. Sampling past such a check helps, but the estimate on which a study finally stops can still be too small.

The remedies are a narrower target, a larger minimum pilot sample, or both.

r_sim_40 <- seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, width = 0.5,
                                   G = 200, seed = 113, m_0 = 40)
r_sim_40[r_sim_40$term %in% c("mean_n", "coverage", "pct_variance_unusable"), ]
#> term                   value
#> mean_n                 43.355
#> coverage               0.9
#> pct_variance_unusable  0

With at least 40 pairs before the first check, coverage in these replications rose to 90 percent (standard error 2 percentage points), at a mean of 43.4 pairs. That is better and still short of 95.

Coverage is not a property of the width alone. It depends on the true value as well, because a strong relationship is estimated with so little sampling error that the rule is met in a small sample at a width that would be narrow for a moderate one. The measured values in the Details of ?seq_aipe_r_sensitivity (95 percent intervals, default pilot, normal data unless stated, at least 800 replications per condition) show the pattern across the family. The sample size n counts pairs for the correlation and the slope, observations for the coefficient of variation, and participants per group for the standardized mean difference.

Effect size and true value Width Mean final n Coverage
Correlation, 0.4 0.4 55 0.78
Correlation, 0.4 0.1 1,079 0.95
Correlation, 0.9 0.1 75 0.45
Correlation, 0.9 0.025 819 0.90
Regression slope, 0.5 0.4 80 0.83
Regression slope, 2 0.2 217 0.61
Coefficient of variation, 0.5, lognormal data 0.2 62 0.79
Coefficient of variation, 0.5, lognormal data 0.05 1,561 0.90
Standardized mean difference, 0.5 0.4 199 0.95

The squared multiple correlation behaves the same way, and worse with many predictors. With five predictors, multivariate normal data, and a population value of 0.50, coverage of its default interval was 0.851 at a width of 0.30, 0.912 at 0.20, 0.936 at 0.10, and 0.949 at 0.05. It falls much further when the number of predictors is not small beside the sample size that the width calls for: for the same population value, coverage was 0.865 with 10 predictors and 0.790 with 15 at a width of 0.20, and 0.668 with 10 and 0.361 with 15 at a width of 0.30. (All of these are from 10,000 replications per condition, reported in ?seq_aipe_R2.) The sample value overestimates the population value by more as predictors are added, the interval is built around it, and the stopping rule does not correct for it. The interval rests on normal theory besides, and is too narrow for heavy tailed data however large the sample.

Before relying on an interval at a planned width, run the sensitivity function at every true value that is plausible for the study, the strongest included, and read its coverage row. vignette("sensitivity-analysis", package = "SMSD") works through such an analysis.

The Classical Procedures

The fixed width (seq_fwd_*, ts_fwd_*), bounded length (seq_blci_*), bounded risk (seq_br_*, ts_br_*), and minimum risk (seq_mr_* for a mean or a location) functions implement procedures for a mean, a median, or the location of a negative exponential distribution that are treated in Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009). They are the older relatives of the procedures above. The two stage fixed width interval is Stein’s (1945), and it is exact for normal data; Chow and Robbins (1965) gave the asymptotic theory of purely sequential fixed width intervals for a mean. Minimum risk point estimation, in which the cost of sampling is set against the cost of estimation error, is credited by Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009, Section 6.4) to Robbins (1959).

Stein’s Two Stage Procedure and the Purely Sequential Rule

A training director wants the mean score on a 100 point skills assessment to within 2 points, with 95 percent confidence. If the standard deviation were known to be 8, the sample size would be known too.

n_known <- seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal(variance = 8^2, d = d)
n_known
#> [1] 62

The standard deviation is not known. Stein’s two stage procedure estimates the variance once, from a first stage, and that estimate fixes the total sample size. Here the 150 simulated scores from above (mean 70, standard deviation 8) stand for the trainees in the order they are assessed.

m <- ts_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d = d)
first_stage <- scores[1:m]
stein <- ts_fwd_norm_mean(first_stage, d = d)
total_n <- attr(stein, "criterion_n")
c(first_stage = m, total = total_n)
#> first_stage       total 
#>          10          75
ts_fwd_norm_mean(first_stage, scores[(m + 1):total_n], d = d)
#> Sequential check (two stage fixed width interval (normal mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 75
#>   Criterion n     : 75
#>   Target width    : 4
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 68.66762
#>   mean              : 70.66762
#>   upper_limit       : 72.66762
#>   optimal_n         : 75
#>   current_n         : 75
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

The purely sequential rule estimates the variance again after every observation and stops the first time the sample size reaches what the current estimate calls for. seq_path() applies it to the same scores, starting at the pilot sample size, and seq_report() words the result.

path <- seq_path(seq_fwd_norm_mean, scores, d = d)
attr(path, "stop_n")
#> [1] 63
plot(path, which = "criterion")

seq_report(path)
#> Sample size was determined with the sequential fixed width confidence
#> interval procedure for the mean of a normal distribution (Mukhopadhyay
#> & de Silva, 2009), with a target full width of 4 for the 95% confidence
#> interval. The stopping rule was evaluated from the pilot sample size (n
#> = 10) onward, after each additional observation, and was first met at n
#> = 63. At that sample size the estimate of the mean was 71.618, 95% CI
#> [69.618, 73.618].
#> 
#> Reference
#> Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and
#>     their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

In this run the purely sequential rule stopped at 63 observations, next to the 62 that a known variance would allow, and Stein’s procedure asked for 75. The difference is not an accident of the sample. Stein’s procedure pays for estimating the variance from the first stage alone through a t quantile on m − 1 degrees of freedom in place of the normal quantile, so its expected total sample size is about t2 / z2 times the known variance sample size: 1.33 for the first stage of 10 used here, 1.09 for a first stage of 30, and 42 for a first stage of 2, which is why ts_fwd_norm_mean_pilot() does not return a very small one.

What the extra observations buy is the guarantee. For normal data Stein’s interval covers the mean with probability at least the confidence level for every mean, every variance, every half width, and every first stage of two or more observations. The purely sequential rule reaches the confidence level only in the limit as the half width shrinks; with about 61 observations needed, as here, its coverage in simulation was 0.938 (the first row of the second table below). One procedure gives an exact guarantee at the price of a larger sample; the other gives a sample close to the known variance one at the price of a guarantee that is only approximate.

What Each Classical Procedure Guarantees

The two stage procedures take the first stage in pilot_data and the second in additional_data; the first stage alone fixes the total sample size, which is the row optimal_n. In the table m is the first stage size and n* the sample size that would be used if the unknown variance, scale, or mean were known.

Function Target Guarantee Price or shortfall
ts_fwd_norm_mean() Interval of half width d for a normal mean (Stein, 1945) Exact: coverage at least the confidence level for normal data, for any m of 2 or more Expected total about t2 / z2 times n*: 1.33 at the default m of 10
ts_fwd_nexp_mean() Interval of full width d for the location of a negative exponential distribution Exact for negative exponential data, for any m of 2 or more Expected total about 1.19 times n* at the default m of 10
ts_br_norm_mean() Risk of the mean at most w for normal data Exact for normal data, for any m of at least k + 2 For squared error, expected total about (m − 1) / (m − 3) times n*: 1.29 at the default m of 10
ts_br_exp_mean() Risk of the mean at most w for exponential data Computed, not proved: in exact calculation for m from 3 to 100 and n* from 1 to 2,000 the risk was at most 0.990 of the bound Expected total about 1.46 times n* at the default m of 20, and 9.04 times at an m of 3
ts_fwd_dfr_mean() Interval of half width d for a mean, no distribution assumed Asymptotic in m Coverage at a nominal 0.95 with the default m of 30: for normal data it tends to 0.940 as the target narrows; in simulation with an n* of 384 and of 1,537 it was 0.915 and 0.917 for exponential data and 0.874 and 0.876 for lognormal data with skewness 4

ts_br_exp_mean() is the two stage procedure that Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009, Sections 8.3.1 and 8.3.2, Equations 8.3.9, 8.3.11, and 8.3.13) attribute to Mukhopadhyay and Pepe (2006), with the constant 0.565 that they attribute to Zacks and Mukhopadhyay (2006). The distribution free two stage interval is the one to be careful with. It treats the first stage variance as if it were the population variance. Once the sample size needed is well beyond the first stage, its coverage is therefore below the nominal level whatever the first stage size: for normal data it tends, as the target narrows, to the probability that a t variable on m − 1 degrees of freedom lies within plus and minus z (0.918 at a nominal 0.95 for a first stage of 10, 0.940 for 30, 0.947 for 100), and it is lower still for skewed data. Only when the first stage is already about as large as the sample size needed, or larger, is the coverage at or above the nominal level.

The purely sequential procedures take the observations so far in x and are checked after each new observation or batch. All of their guarantees are asymptotic: they hold in the limit as the precision target tightens or the cost of an observation falls, so that the sample size needed, n*, grows.

Function Target Measured with the default pilot
seq_fwd_norm_mean() Interval of half width d for a normal mean Coverage at a nominal 0.95: 0.933 at an n* of about 15, lowest (about 0.922) at 24 to 28, 0.938 at about 61, 0.949 at about 246
seq_fwd_dfr_mean() Interval of half width d for a mean, no distribution assumed Normal data: 0.935, 0.942, and 0.948 at an n* of about 15, 61, and 246. Exponential data: lowest (about 0.855) at 40 to 61, 0.934 at about 246, 0.946 at about 983
seq_fwd_nexp_mean() Interval of full width d for the location of a negative exponential distribution 0.938 at an n* of about 15, lowest (about 0.930) at 25, 0.948 at about 240
seq_blci_dfr_median() Interval for a median between two order statistics, of length at most 2 d At a fixed sample size, at least the confidence level. As a sequential procedure at a nominal 0.95: 0.918 to 0.947 for normal, exponential, and Cauchy data with n* from 25 to 800; a check whose rule is met prints a note saying so
seq_br_norm_mean() Risk of the mean at most w for normal data Squared error: risk 1.11 times the bound when the bound calls for 15 observations, highest (about 1.22 times) at 25 to 30, 1.05 times at 100, 1.01 times at 400
seq_mr_norm_mean() Minimum risk for a normal mean (Robbins, 1959) Standard deviation of 1: risk 1.07, 1.06, 1.04, 1.01, and 1.00 times the minimum at an n* of 10, 15, 20, 50, and 100
seq_mr_exp_mean() Minimum risk for an exponential mean Mean of 1: risk 1.08, 1.16, 1.15, 1.05, and 1.02 times the minimum at an n* of 10, 15, 20, 50, and 100
seq_mr_nexp_mean() Minimum risk for the location of a negative exponential distribution Risk 1.00 to 1.03 times the minimum in ten of twelve conditions (n* from 18 to 387); 1.04 and 1.09 times in the other two (n* of 18 and 9)
seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb() Minimum risk for a mean, no distribution assumed Exponential data with n* of 25, 100, and 300: risk 1.02, 1.02, and 1.01 times the minimum

The ratios in the first table are computed here from the formulas on the help pages. Every simulated figure in the two tables is quoted from the help page of the function, which gives the conditions in full (40,000 or more simulated studies per condition for the purely sequential procedures, 20,000 for ts_fwd_dfr_mean()). The tables show two patterns. For the fixed width intervals for a mean or a location and for the bounded risk procedure, the shortfall is largest not at the widest targets but where the sample size needed is a few times the pilot sample size: an early underestimate of the variance can then end the sampling, and the pilot is too small a part of the sample to protect against it. And skewness slows the approach to the nominal level considerably, for the purely sequential distribution free interval as for the two stage one.

Data with no variation are never reported as a stopping rule that is met on the strength of a variance of zero. When every observation is equal, or equal to ten significant digits, the seven purely sequential functions that estimate a spread report the rule as not met and set the attribute variance_unusable to TRUE, a deliberate departure from the rules as printed, under which sampling would stop at once. The four two stage functions that estimate a spread stop with an error instead, because no second stage could change a total sample size that the first stage alone determines. The median interval estimates no variance: for it, heavily tied data can give an interval of length zero, which meets the rule.

Each procedure has a pilot function, named with the suffix _pilot. The classical pilots take the procedure’s own arguments, then a minimum size m_0, then a tuning constant gamma. For the two stage procedures the minimum matters more than the rule, as the ratios for Stein’s procedure show. When the population variance is known, seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal() gives the sample size for the fixed width interval directly.

Where the Budget Constrained Procedure Fits

The AIPE procedures stop when an interval is narrow enough, whatever that costs. seq_budget() starts from the other end: the total cost is fixed, the populations differ in what an observation costs, and the question is how to divide the budget so that a contrast of the population means is estimated as precisely as it can be. Luh and Guo (2016) planned such a study with a fixed sample size, taking the unknown variances from a separate pilot study; Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025) made the plan sequential, so that it needs no advance values of the standard deviations and pays for its pilot observations from the same budget.

For populations with contrast weights ci, standard deviations σi, and costs ai per observation, and a budget A0, the allocation that minimizes the variance of the contrast estimate (Theorem 1 of the article, its Equation 12) gives population i

ni0 = A0 |ci| σi / (√ai × Σl |cl| σl √al)

observations: more when its weight in the contrast is larger, when its scores vary more, and when it is cheaper to sample. Suppose a survey compares mean household spending in rural households with the average of metropolitan and suburban households, a completed rural interview costs 120, a metropolitan one 40, and a suburban one 60, and the three standard deviations are thought to be equal.

plan <- seq_budget_optimal(
  contrast_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),
  sigmas           = c(20, 20, 20),
  cost_per_group   = c(120, 40, 60),
  budget           = 30000
)
round(plan$n_per_group, 1)
#> [1] 152.2 131.8 107.6

The rural group carries twice the weight of each of the others and, at equal costs, would receive twice the observations. Because a rural interview costs three times a metropolitan one, it receives 1.15 times as many as the metropolitan group. The sequential procedure replaces the supposed standard deviations with the sample standard deviations and looks again after each observation; vignette("seq-budget", package = "SMSD") works through it, with the tests of noninferiority and equivalence that the article develops.

The procedure assumes independent observations within each population, at a known cost per observation. It fits comparisons of groups, strata, or regions whose unit costs differ. It does not model clustering: when observations are collected in clusters whose members resemble one another, as in a multistage survey, the variance of the contrast is not the one the allocation minimizes. Survey statisticians have adaptive designs of their own, among them adaptive cluster sampling (Thompson, 1990) and adaptive survey designs, in which sample units are treated differently so as to get the best quality of response that the costs allow (Schouten, Calinescu, & Luiten, 2013). Those adapt which units are sampled or how they are approached; seq_budget() adapts how many observations each population receives.
